# Rāhula Saṁyutta (SN 18)
**ID:** SN 18
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Rāhula Saṁyutta* (SN 18; also spelled *Rāhulasaṁyutta*), titled the "Linked Discourses with Rāhula," is the eighteenth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. Set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthī, the collection opens with the Venerable Rāhula—the son of the Buddha, who was ordained as a novice during the Buddha's first return to Kapilavatthu—approaching the Buddha to ask for a concise Dhamma teaching so that he might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, and ardent [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x]. The samyutta comprises twenty-two short discourses arranged in two chapters (*vagga*s) [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. While classified under the programmatic heading of a "Specific Person," the text provides virtually no personal or narrative detail, functioning instead as a strictly doctrinal exposition focused on the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anattā*) [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x].
Throughout the collection, the Buddha interrogates Rāhula across fifty-nine doctrinal categories [Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Williams, Critical Concepts]. These encompass the six internal sense bases and six external sense objects, followed by six classes each of consciousness (*viññāṇa*), contact (*samphassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), volition (*sañcetanā*), and craving (*taṇhā*), as well as the six elements (*dhātu*) and the five aggregates (*khandha*) [Williams, Critical Concepts]. Early discourses enumerate consecutive pentads of mental factors (*phassa-pañcamā*) [Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012]. Applying the standard catechetical formula to these categories demonstrates that conditioned phenomena are not fit to be regarded as "mine," "I am," or "myself," thereby leading the practitioner to revulsion (*nibbidā*), dispassion (*virāga*), and liberation (*vimutti*) [Bodhi 2003_x; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify corresponding discourses in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99), including SĀ 23 and SĀ 198 for the *Anusayasutta* (SN 18.21), and SĀ 24 and SĀ 199 for the *Apagatasutta* (SN 18.22) [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse computation by DharmaNexus agrees with alignments to the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and further aligns shared formulaic material with the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100), the *Madhyamāgama* (T 26), and Śamathadeva's Tibetan *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094) [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus identifies thousands of matching passages, sharing extensive formulaic material most notably with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Diṭṭhi Saṁyutta* (SN 24), the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), and the *Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 147) [DharmaNexus].
